content.title: About
content.content: Beef jerky is dried, seasoned strips of lean beef that are marinated in a blend of spices and then slowly dried at low temperature. The result is a dense, flavorful, long‑lasting snack with a characteristic salty‑spicy taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef jerky originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient way to preserve meat for travel and outdoor trips.
Traditionally, lean cuts of beef are used to keep fat content low and extend shelf life.
Protein content in jerky can reach up to 50 % of the product’s weight.
Different brands use unique spice blends, ranging from classic black pepper to smoked chipotle.
Jerky is often included in athletes’ diets as a quick source of amino acids.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Jerky provides a concentrated source of complete protein, essential for muscle repair and metabolic function.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Unlike many snack foods, jerky contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is vital for normal blood formation and nervous system health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Jerky is often salty; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some varieties contain nitrites or artificial flavorings, which may be undesirable for sensitive individuals.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rarely, people can have an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Certain jerky products are made from fattier cuts, increasing calorie density.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beef jerky is convenient as a standalone snack, can be added to salads, soups, or used in dishes like fried rice. Break it into smaller pieces to top meals or simply enjoy straight from the pack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store jerky in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Once opened, keep it in the refrigerator to maintain crispness and prevent mold growth. Shelf life is usually indicated on the packaging.

chicken-drumstick-rotisserie-skin-not-ea.title: Chicken drumstick, rotisserie, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken drumsticks cooked on a rotisserie are the thigh meat of the bird, usually served without skin. Rotisserie cooking provides even heat and a characteristic smoky flavor. The meat is tender, juicy, high in protein and relatively low in fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks are a staple in fast‑food and street‑food dishes.
Rotisserie cooking requires little added oil, making the product leaner.
Chicken was domesticated over 8,000 years ago and is one of the most widely kept livestock species.
Removing the skin cuts saturated fat content, creating a more diet‑friendly option.
Dark meat contains more iron than white breast meat.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Drumsticks provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The product contains virtually no carbs, suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: It provides zinc, phosphorus and iron, important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Reduced fat when skin is removed
items.content: Skipping the skin dramatically lowers saturated fat and calorie content.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken meat.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: Pre‑seasoned drumsticks often contain added salt, increasing sodium intake.

items.title: Cholesterol if skin is eaten
items.content: Consuming the skin raises saturated fat and cholesterol levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skin‑less drumsticks can be eaten hot, added to salads, soups, stews, or used in sandwiches. They are easy to slice for quick‑prep meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C up to 3 months. Ensure the meat is thoroughly reheated before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken with gravy is a dish made from boiled or roasted chicken served under a flavorful sauce made from broth, cream, or flour. It is popular in Russian and European cuisines, offering a tender taste and juicy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken is one of the most consumed meats worldwide.
Traditional gravy is prepared from chicken broth made by simmering bones and vegetables.
Regional variations may include mushrooms, onions, carrots, or spices such as bay leaf and black pepper.
The dish is often served with mashed potatoes, rice, or pasta.
Chicken bones used for broth are rich in collagen, which gives the sauce body.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with red meat, chicken contains less saturated fat, making it a heart‑friendlier option.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin, vitamin B6, and B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It contains phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones and immunity.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Gravy made from broth helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared gravies often contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Fat in the sauce
items.content: Gravies made with cream or butter increase calories and saturated fat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot chicken with gravy alongside mashed potatoes, rice, pasta, or vegetables. Garnish with fresh herbs for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly to a boil before serving to eliminate any bacteria.

content.title: About
content.content: Hard plain pretzels are a baked snack made from wheat flour, water, yeast and a pinch of salt. After shaping, they are briefly dipped in a lye solution, which gives them their characteristic golden‑brown crust and a crisp bite. They have a subtle salty flavor and a crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pretzels originated in Germany, where they were called "Brezel".
The twisted knot shape is said to represent the crossed arms of monks in prayer.
In the United States pretzels became popular in the early 20th century thanks to German immigrants.
The hard variety was developed later to provide a longer‑lasting, crunchy snack.
A light dusting of salt not only adds flavor but also helps preserve the product.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Hard pretzels typically contain less fat than soft varieties, making them a lighter snack option.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat flour provides quick‑acting energy, useful before physical activity.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: In modest amounts pretzels can contribute to maintaining normal iron levels.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain versions are a good source of fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Mild salt for electrolyte balance
items.content: A light sprinkle of salt can help replenish electrolytes after sweating.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Pretzels made from wheat flour may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Even a light salt coating can add up if pretzels are eaten frequently.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While low in fat, the carbohydrate content makes pretzels relatively calorie‑dense.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: The hard, crunchy texture can pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pretzels are convenient as a stand‑alone snack, paired with cheese, hummus, nut butter, or added to salads. A quick warm‑up in the oven can enhance their aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep pretzels in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, refrigerate to maintain crispness. Discard any that develop mold or an off smell.

tea-iced-instant-black-pre-sweetened-wit.title: Iced Instant Black Tea Sweetened with Low‑Calorie Sweetener

content.title: About
content.content: This instant black tea is designed for making a cold beverage. It is already sweetened with a low‑calorie sweetener (5249), so no additional sugar is needed. It dissolves quickly in cold water while preserving the characteristic aroma of black tea.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black tea is the second most consumed beverage worldwide after water.
Instant tea was invented in the early 20th century for convenience.
Low‑calorie sweeteners allow a reduction in energy content without sacrificing sweetness.
Iced tea is especially popular in summer, often served with lemon or mint.
The instant dissolution technology retains most of the polyphenols typical of black tea.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Black tea is rich in polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Moderate regular consumption may improve vascular function.

items.title: Enhanced focus
items.content: Caffeine in black tea boosts alertness and concentration.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: The 5249 sweetener contributes virtually no calories, making the drink diet‑friendly.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Iced tea helps maintain fluid balance, especially in hot weather.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Allergy to sweetener
items.content: Rarely, an individual may be intolerant to the specific low‑calorie sweetener used.

items.title: Tannin content
items.content: High tannin levels can reduce iron absorption when tea is consumed in large amounts.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Place 1 sachet (or 1‑2 g) into 200 ml of cold water, stir thoroughly until fully dissolved. Optionally add a slice of lemon, fresh mint, or ice cubes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the sachet tightly sealed to prevent moisture.
